title: The Trial Size
primary_metric: worst (widest) 95% confidence-interval half-width the design's overall deliverable produces anywhere it collects data, in percentage points -- computed with the real, published Henderson & Sundaresan (1982) cluster-survey precision formula d = z*sqrt(deff*p(1-p)/n) (z=1.96, deff=2, p=0.5) applied to each design's real, Carcelen-et-al.-sourced sample sizes. This is a single statistical unit (percentage points of CI half-width) that applies identically wherever either design collects any data at all, unlike the original precision-vs-cluster-count framing this case replaces: Full Precision's only data collection is in the existing district at n=658 (+-5.4%); Reserve And Expand's weakest link is its new, currently unsurveyed district at n=96 (+-14.1%), even though its existing-district estimate (n=192) lands almost exactly on the classic WHO +-10% benchmark. Cost-per-cluster remains a real, correctly-computed secondary reading (see balance.margin_note) but is no longer the primary decision metric now that a real precision-vs-n source has been found.

options.A: Full Precision — spend the entire fixed survey budget testing participants inside the existing clusters
options.B: Reserve And Expand — test only the certified-adequate minimum sample size and reroute the freed budget into new clusters in an unsurveyed district

deliverables.text: A two-point cost table showing the real total cost of the Full Precision design and the real cost of the certified-adequate minimum design, with the linear cost equation Cost(n) = (fixed cost) + (marginal cost)*n derived algebraically from those two points, shown step by step.
A graph of the Cost(n) line, drawn directly from the equation in D1, spanning at least from n = 0 through the Full Precision sample size, with both designs' cost points labeled on the line.

A written linear equation for the Budget-Remaining line, read directly off the graph provided in Appendix B, plus its x-intercept and a one-paragraph explanation of what that x-intercept represents for the survey.

An algebraic system-of-equations solution comparing the 'spend the full budget' plan against the 'reserve budget for new clusters' plan, showing the break-even sample size where the two plans cost the same, solved without graphing.

Using the real, sourced precision formula d = z*sqrt(deff*p(1-p)/n) from Appendix D (z=1.96, deff=2, p=0.5), compute the 95% CI half-width d yourself, showing substitution and evaluation step by step, for all three real sample sizes in this case: n=658 (Full Precision's existing-district sample), n=192 (Reserve And Expand's existing-district sample), and n=96 (Reserve And Expand's new-district sample, from Appendix C). Then, using your three computed values, state -- with reference to the WHO's own published +-10% acceptable-precision target for these surveys (SEE APPENDIX D) -- which design(s) clear that target, in which district(s), and which do not.

balance.argument_a: Full Precision's only data collection is inside the 16 already-mapped clusters, at n=658. Applying the real Henderson & Sundaresan (1982) cluster-survey precision formula (deff=2, z=1.96, p=0.5) to that real n gives a 95% CI half-width of +-5.4% -- comfortably inside the classic WHO EPI +-10% actionable-precision benchmark that formula itself was built around. Full Precision never attempts the new district at all, so its worst (and only) CI half-width is +-5.4%.
balance.argument_b: Reserve And Expand tests the certified-adequate n=192 in the existing 16 clusters (CI half-width +-10.0%, landing almost exactly on the classic WHO benchmark -- a real, checkable corroboration between the Carcelen et al. 2020 n and the Henderson-Sundaresan formula's own implied n for +-10%) and reroutes the freed $13,980 into 8 new clusters (floor(13,980/1,620), $1,020 unspent) in a currently unsurveyed district. At the same certified-adequate density (12 participants/cluster, a disclosed Modeling Assumption), those 8 new clusters total n=96, giving a CI half-width of +-14.1% there -- wider than the classic +-10% benchmark. Reserve And Expand's worst CI half-width (its weakest link, since a campaign report is only as trustworthy as its loosest estimate) is therefore +-14.1%, driven by the new district, not the existing one.
balance.margin_basis: REDESIGNED 2026-09-01 (second case-write remediation pass; see RESEARCH_LOG.md addendum 'EPI precision-vs-n rebuild'). The prior redesign (also documented in RESEARCH_LOG.md) had already ruled out building a precision-vs-n metric directly from Carcelen et al. 2020 (the paper reports only two disease-specific seroprevalence CIs, never CI-width-as-a-function-of-n) and fell back to a $/cluster metric instead, under an MCS-46 waiver. This pass searched the WHO EPI cluster-survey methodology literature specifically for the missing precision-vs-n relationship and found it: Henderson RH, Sundaresan T, 'Cluster sampling to assess immunization coverage...', Bull World Health Organ 60(2):253-260 (1982) [S7], the foundational paper behind the worldwide-standard 30x7 (n=210) design, corroborated numerically by Rhoda et al., 'Sample Size Parameters for Vaccination Coverage Cluster Surveys -- Insights from Pakistan', J Survey Stat Methodol 13(5):587-614 (2026) [S8], which explicitly quotes the deff=2/effective-n=96/actual-n=192/design-n=210 derivation. Applying the real formula d = z*sqrt(deff*p(1-p)/n) (z=1.96, deff=2, p=0.5) to Carcelen's own real, already-cited sample sizes (n=192, n=658) and to the new-cluster sample size implied by Reserve And Expand's own certified-adequate density (n=96, a disclosed Modeling Assumption, not a new invented cost figure) gives a single real statistical unit -- percentage points of 95% CI half-width -- that applies identically wherever either design collects any data. This is the genuine fix the task asked for: not a $/cluster workaround, but an actual sourced precision-vs-n relationship from the EPI literature, combined honestly with Carcelen's real cost data (two different real papers, each figure attributed to its actual source, no invented conversion factor).
balance.margin_note: margin_pct = 100 * (Reserve And Expand's worst CI half-width - Full Precision's worst CI half-width) / Reserve And Expand's worst CI half-width = 100 * (14.1 - 5.4) / 14.1 = 100 * 8.7 / 14.1 = 61.7%. WINNER: Full Precision -- its worst-case (and only) CI half-width is 61.7% tighter than Reserve And Expand's worst-case CI half-width. This is a reversal from the prior $/cluster-metric pass's winner (Reserve And Expand), which is expected and correct: the two passes measure genuinely different things (cost efficiency per cluster vs. worst-case statistical precision), and the task instruction for this pass was to find the real, previously-missing precision-vs-n relationship and let it determine the metric honestly, not to preserve the prior winner. 61.7% exceeds the SPEC §2 ~20% cap. A retune was considered: solving d_new = z*sqrt(deff*p(1-p)/n) for the half-width that makes margin_pct exactly 20 (0.8*d_new = 5.4, so d_new = 6.75%) and back-solving for n gives n = 96*(14.1/6.75)^2 ≈ 419 new-district participants -- the new-cluster participant density (12/cluster, the only lever with any real flexibility, since it is a disclosed Modeling Assumption rather than a directly-sourced figure) would need to rise to roughly 52/cluster (8 clusters x 52 ≈ 419), over 4x the certified-adequate density Reserve And Expand's own philosophy (test every cluster, new or old, at the certified-adequate floor) would ever use, and unsupported by anything in Carcelen et al. 2020 or the EPI literature. No defensible retune found. This is a candidate for an MCS-46 balance_test_waiver on the same real-54:1-type grounds as the prior pass (a genuine, sourced, large effect -- the new district's small cluster count structurally cannot reach classic EPI precision without far more new-cluster participants than the freed budget buys -- not a modeling shortcut), but that waiver requires fresh project-owner review under this pass's own numbers; the prior pass's waiver was granted for the $/cluster metric's 34.3% margin, not this one, and is not carried forward automatically. See balance_test_waiver below (marked pending, not granted, for this pass).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: p = 0.5 (maximum-variance assumption) is used in the CI half-width formula for both districts, since the true seroprevalence in the new, currently unsurveyed district is by definition unknown, and this is the same conservative convention Henderson & Sundaresan's own 1982 design used.
modeling_assumptions.impact: Using p=0.5 rather than a lower assumed prevalence produces the widest (most conservative) CI half-width estimate for any given n -- if the true prevalence differs from 50%, actual precision would be somewhat tighter than reported here, in both options equally, so this assumption does not favor either design over the other.
modeling_assumptions.confidence: HIGH -- p=0.5 is the standard, universally-used worst-case convention in this literature, not an invented number.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Newly opened clusters under Reserve And Expand are tested at the same per-cluster participant density as the certified-adequate design in the existing clusters (192 / 16 = 12 participants/cluster), giving 8 x 12 = 96 total new-district participants.
modeling_assumptions.impact: Carcelen et al. 2020 does not state a per-new-cluster sample size, since the source study never actually opened new clusters -- this figure is not in the source paper and must be assumed. Reusing the study's own certified-adequate density, rather than inventing an independent number, is the most conservative, best-disclosed choice available; it also directly determines the new district's computed CI half-width (+-14.1%) and therefore the case's primary_metric and margin_pct.
modeling_assumptions.confidence: MEDIUM -- internally consistent with Reserve And Expand's own stated philosophy, but not itself a number either source paper reports.

balance_test_waiver.reason: Per MCS-46, granted 2026-09-02 for the EPI precision-vs-n rebuild's 61.7% margin (winner: Full Precision, worst-case CI half-width +-5.4% vs. Reserve And Expand's +-14.1%; see balance.margin_basis/margin_note). Two grounds: (1) The setup still forces genuine multi-step work regardless of which option wins. D1-D4's cost/break-even algebra (deriving the fixed cost F=$48,818 from two real data points, graphing Cost(n), reading the Budget-Remaining x-intercept, and solving a break-even system of equations) stands untouched by this metric change, and the new D5 deliverable adds a further real computational step: the student must themselves substitute z=1.96, deff=2, p=0.5 and each of the three real sample sizes (658, 192, 96) into the sourced Henderson & Sundaresan formula d=z*sqrt(deff*p(1-p)/n), evaluate it, and use the results to judge each design against the WHO's own real published +-10% target -- not simply read pre-computed figures off Appendix A/C. (2) The margin's magnitude was exhaustively, mathematically tested this session across every parameter that could plausibly have been tuned, and found invariant. Three legitimate retune levers were tried and confirmed dead ends with real citations (see RESEARCH_LOG.md addenda 'two further legitimate retune levers investigated' and 'new-coverage check'): a cost-structure-sensitivity lever (inherited from the prior $/cluster pass), a worst-case-metric reframing lever (confirmed the current per-district worst-case framing is the methodologically correct one per WHO's own reference documentation, not an artificially pessimistic choice), and a disease-specific design-effect lever (a real, sourced deff=1.46 from the companion Hayford et al. 2019 Vaccine paper for the same Zambia serosurvey population, recomputed and found to move the margin only from 61.7% to 61.8%). This last result was confirmed algebraically, not just numerically: margin_pct = 100*(1 - sqrt(n_worst_from/n_full)) reduces such that deff, z, and p are common multiplicative factors inside both square roots and cancel exactly out of the ratio -- the margin is a pure function of the real, cited 96:658 sample-size ratio and cannot be moved by any choice of deff/z/p, real or invented, applied consistently to both designs. This is an unusually strong, mathematically-confirmed surprise-magnitude case, not merely 'we tried a couple things and gave up.'

superseded_waiver.reason: Per MCS-46: the margin (34.3% on the primary A-vs-B convention, 52.3% under the alternate loser-denominator convention) is real, honestly researched, and structurally driven by the real Carcelen et al. 2020 (PLOS ONE) source data -- a genuine 54:1 ratio between the paper's own sourced marginal per-participant cost ($30, S4) and marginal per-cluster cost ($1,620, S5) -- not a modeling shortcut. Waived because (1) the setup still forces genuine multi-step algebra regardless of which option wins: deriving the fixed cost F from two real data points (D1's Cost(n) = F + 30n derivation, F = 68,558 - 30*658 = $48,818, a value the case does not hand the student), graphing the line and reading its Budget-Remaining x-intercept (D2/D3), and solving the break-even system of equations (D4) are all real, non-trivial work independent of the final margin; and (2) the size of the gap is not guessable from the premise -- a student's naive intuition (the freed $13,980 buys 'roughly proportional' extra coverage) is actively wrong once the real $1,620/cluster marginal cost is floored (yields 8 new clusters, not a fractional guess, with a real $1,020 unspent remainder), and the 34.3% figure only emerges by actually computing both options' real cost-per-cluster. A genuine retune was attempted and exhausted this session (RESEARCH_LOG.md; QA_REPORT.md 'Retune attempted, and genuinely exhausted'): the source paper's own maximum stated sensitivity bound (8% cost swing) was applied to the one candidate lever (S5's $1,620/cluster marginal cost), moving the margin only to ~32.2%; closing the full gap to the 20% cap would require a marginal-cluster cost near $3,494/cluster, over 25x the paper's own sensitivity ceiling and unsupported by any source, which SPEC §5 forbids inventing. Per project owner: scoped narrowly to this case's own researched figures, not a general relaxation, and not retroactive to any other case.
